title: Developer Behind AI-Built Adobe Clones Says They Are Not Ready
excerpt: Brandon Thomas promised 100% parity in a month on Reddit, then called his seven ArtCraft apps 'super early alpha' on Hacker News — and the documentation backs the caution.
body:
• Atlanta developer Brandon Thomas released seven free, open-source clones of Adobe apps — for Photoshop, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, Illustrator, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro — built in Rust with Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Thomas himself calls them "not anywhere close to ready" and "super early alpha" on Hacker News, despite promising on Reddit that they would reach "100% parity within a month."
  • The project's own documentation is more measured: FilmCraft claims roughly 86-87% feature-checklist coverage but only about 50-60% readiness for real projects.
  • For working creatives, the practical takeaway is to experiment on personal projects, not deadlines — established free tools such as GIMP and DaVinci Resolve remain the safer switch today.

The developer behind a set of AI-built clones of Adobe's creative software has given his own products the clearest warning label they have received: they are, in his words, "not anywhere close to ready."

Brandon Thomas, founder of ArtCraft, released seven free, open-source applications modelled on Photoshop, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, Illustrator, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro. The clones — PhotoCraft, FilmCraft, LightCraft, VectorCraft, EffectCraft, DesignCraft and PrintCraft — were built in Rust using Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, Thomas said in his Reddit announcement, as reported by Digital Trends and Gizmodo.

"We're going to reach 100% parity within a month."

— Brandon Thomas, ArtCraft founder, on Reddit

Two messages, a month apart in ambition

On Reddit, Thomas was expansive. "I've vibe coded replacements to 7 of Adobe's apps in Rust," he wrote on X, and in a Reddit comment he promised 100% parity within a month.

On Hacker News, the tone was different. There Thomas described the apps as "super early alpha" and said they were "not anywhere close to ready," Digital Trends and Gizmodo reported. He invited developers to contribute and said he would pay bug bounties. In other Hacker News comments cited by TechSpot, he put 99% parity at months rather than years — a retreat from the one-month claim, but still an aggressive timetable for software Adobe has built over decades.

Thomas said he needed the launch to build a community. "I needed to seed a community that could help contribute bug reports and PRs," he wrote on Hacker News. By October 9, GitHub contributor data listed 230 distinct accounts beyond Thomas across the seven repositories, Digital Trends reported.

What hands-on testing found

Gizmodo tested PhotoCraft, the Photoshop clone, and found the layout familiar: lasso, feathering, paste, levels and colour tools were where an Adobe user would expect them. The Free Transform function was not. Escaping from it did not work, then it undid itself, then the same steps worked for no clear reason, the reviewer wrote.

Digital Trends tried PhotoCraft for basic tasks including background removal and found it worked for that narrow test. Its wider assessment came from the project's own documentation. PhotoCraft's README says it is not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work, and its October 7 release notes list incomplete tools, performance gaps and settings that do nothing. A safer-save fix, protecting existing files when a save is interrupted, was merged on October 5.

FilmCraft's documentation makes the gap explicit in numbers: roughly 87% feature-checklist coverage, but only 50-60% readiness for real projects. A menu item being wired to a command, Digital Trends noted, measures wiring rather than behaviour.

Why Adobe users were listening

The appeal is the subscription. The clones carry no cancellation fees, and the code can be kept, modified and built independently. Thomas has cited Adobe's cancellation fees as a motivation. TechSpot and Gizmodo both noted the backdrop: the U.S. government sued Adobe in June 2024 over alleged hidden early-termination fees and difficult cancellations, and in March 2026 Adobe agreed to a $150 million settlement, while denying wrongdoing.

Thomas describes himself as a 15-year industry veteran, and Gizmodo quoted his Reddit post citing work on payment systems and robotics. He is founder of ArtCraft, Storyteller.ai and FakeYou, according to his GitHub profile cited by Digital Trends. ArtCraft's paid AI image and video product helps fund the free suite, he said.

What's next

Nothing in the coverage suggests Adobe has taken legal action over the clones, and the reports do not settle whether close imitation of Adobe's interfaces raises copyright, patent or trade-dress issues. That question will decide whether the project lasts.

For now, the author's own rating stands. Experimenters and hobbyists can download the apps today and follow progress in public. Professionals on deadlines have established alternatives — GIMP and Affinity for images, DaVinci Resolve for video — that Digital Trends pointed to. The clones do not need to beat Adobe overnight to matter, but by Thomas's own account, they have not yet earned a place in paid work.
